subtopic_detail: Timing of the first retinopathy of prematurity examination in a preterm infant weaned to room air by day three
stem:
You are the registrar on the neonatal unit preparing a preterm girl for her discharge planning meeting. She is feeding fully from the breast in an open cot and has gained weight steadily over the past fortnight, with no apnoeic or desaturation episodes recorded in that time.

Her cranial ultrasound and newborn hearing screen were both normal, and she has not needed any supplemental oxygen since her first two days of life. Her mother asks which tests still need to be arranged before they go home.

data_table.Current age: 28 days, corrected age 33 weeks and 4 days
data_table.Respiratory support: Continuous positive airway pressure for 48 hours, in room air since day three

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to retinal examination?

options.text: Defer the first examination until she reaches 36 weeks corrected gestational age
options.rationale: The first examination is timed to four weeks after birth or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever falls later, so waiting until 36 weeks would step over the window in which treatable disease usually declares itself. A 36 week timing belongs to a more mature infant being checked for late structural sequelae rather than for evolving disease. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.text: Examine only if she needs supplemental oxygen again before she is discharged
options.rationale: Oxygen exposure modifies risk but does not define eligibility, and disease occurs in preterm infants who never receive supplemental oxygen at all. Eligibility is set by gestation and birthweight, which she meets on both counts. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.text: Arrange the first retinal examination now, at four weeks after her birth
options.rationale: She was born below 31 weeks with a birthweight below 1250 g, so she qualifies for screening, and the first examination falls at four weeks after birth or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later. At 33 weeks and 4 days corrected the four week point governs, which is today. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.text: Arrange one retinal examination on the day her discharge is planned
options.rationale: Screening is a serial process with examinations every one to two weeks until the retina is fully vascularised, not a single snapshot. A single examination tied to a discharge date would miss disease that progresses after she goes home. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity)
source_refs: Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: Omit retinal examination because her birthweight was above one kilogram
options.rationale: The birthweight threshold for screening is 1250 g rather than 1000 g, so a weight of 1180 g sits inside the criteria rather than outside them. Her gestation below 31 weeks would qualify her independently in any case. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

explanation.summary: Retinopathy of prematurity is a proliferative retinal vascular disease of preterm infants whose natural history is time critical, because the treatable stage occupies a narrow window and untreated progression causes retinal detachment and irreversible blindness. Australian screening criteria select infants by gestation below 31 weeks or birthweight below 1250 g, and deliberately do not use oxygen exposure as an entry criterion because disease occurs without it. The first examination is timed at four weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later, which protects the most immature infants from being examined before disease could plausibly appear. Examinations then repeat at one to two week intervals, with the interval determined by the zone and stage found, until vascularisation reaches the periphery.
key_points: Screening eligibility is gestation below 31 weeks or birthweight below 1250 g
Supplemental oxygen exposure modifies risk but is not an entry criterion
First examination at four weeks postnatal or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later
Examinations repeat every one to two weeks until peripheral vascularisation completes
Screening continues after discharge and must be handed over explicitly
explanation.pearls: The later of four weeks postnatal age and 31 weeks postmenstrual age sets the first examination, so a baby born at 24 weeks waits until 31 weeks postmenstrual age while a baby born at 30 weeks is examined at four weeks of age.

sources.label: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity
Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity

subtopic_detail: Febrile encephalopathy with transaminitis in the second week of life without any vesicular rash
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department to see a 9 day old boy who has been feeding poorly since yesterday and is now difficult to rouse. During your assessment he has a two minute focal seizure affecting the right arm.

He was born at term by normal vaginal birth after an uncomplicated pregnancy, and his mother has never had any genital lesions or blistering rash. His skin is examined carefully under good light and shows no vesicles, and his anterior fontanelle is soft. Blood cultures and a lumbar puncture are taken, and empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and cefotaxime are commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178/min, blood pressure 58/34 mmHg, respiratory rate 56/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic between episodes, no rash or vesicles, soft fontanelle, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Blood results: Alanine aminotransferase 640 U/L (less than 45), platelets 74 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count within normal limits
data_table.Cerebrospinal fluid: White cells 68 x10^6/L with lymphocyte predominance, protein 1.4 g/L (0.2-0.8), glucose within normal limits, Gram stain negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to his management?

options.text: Continue the intravenous antibiotics alone and review when the cultures return
options.rationale: A lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid with a negative Gram stain, marked transaminitis and thrombocytopenia points away from a pyogenic bacterial cause that antibiotics alone would cover. Waiting for cultures wastes the interval in which antiviral therapy changes outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.text: Add intravenous ganciclovir and arrange a urine sample for viral culture
options.rationale: Ganciclovir targets cytomegalovirus, which in the congenital form presents at birth with growth restriction, microcephaly and a positive urine test in the first three weeks, not with an acute febrile encephalopathy at day nine. The acute disseminated picture here fits a different virus. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.text: Add intravenous dexamethasone before the next dose of antibiotic is given
options.rationale: Adjunctive corticosteroid is used in older children with proven or suspected Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis and is not recommended in neonates, where evidence of benefit is absent. It would not address the viral process suggested by these results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Add high dose intravenous aciclovir now and send samples for viral testing
options.rationale: Disseminated neonatal herpes presents in the first two weeks with seizures, hepatitis and thrombocytopenia, and fewer than half of affected babies ever develop a rash or have a mother with a known history. Empirical high dose aciclovir is started on suspicion because mortality rises steeply with every hour of delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.text: Withhold antiviral therapy until the cerebrospinal fluid result is available
options.rationale: Cerebrospinal fluid viral testing can be falsely negative early in the illness and takes time to return, so a negative or pending result does not justify withholding therapy. Treatment is started empirically and stopped later if testing and the clinical course exclude the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

explanation.summary: Neonatal herpes simplex infection is acquired around the time of birth and presents in three overlapping patterns: disease limited to skin, eye and mouth, central nervous system disease, and disseminated disease with hepatitis and coagulopathy. The trap for clinicians is that the absence of a maternal history and the absence of vesicles are both common, because most transmission comes from asymptomatic shedding during a first infection the mother never recognised. Any neonate with fever, seizures, an unexplained transaminitis or a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid should receive empirical high dose aciclovir alongside antibacterial cover while testing proceeds. Delay is the main determinant of death and of neurological disability among survivors.
key_points: Most mothers of affected babies have no history of genital herpes
Vesicles are absent in a large proportion at presentation
Unexplained transaminitis with thrombocytopenia suggests disseminated disease
Empirical aciclovir is started on suspicion, not after confirmation
Antibacterial cover continues until bacterial sepsis is excluded
explanation.pearls: Neonatal herpes needs 20 mg/kg of intravenous aciclovir every eight hours, which is well above the dose used in older children, and disseminated or central nervous system disease is treated for at least 21 days.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

subtopic_detail: Operative referral timing once a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with pale stools is established at seven weeks
stem:
A 7 week old girl is reviewed in your general practice because she is still yellow. She was born at term, is exclusively breastfed and is gaining weight along her birth centile.

Her mother has photographed several nappies over the past fortnight, and the stools in them are a pale putty colour while the wet nappies look dark. The split bilirubin you requested last week has returned, and her newborn screening test and thyroid function were both normal. She is alert and feeding well, and there is no bruising.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced sclerae, soft abdomen with a liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, no bruising
data_table.Bilirubin: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 92 micromol/L
data_table.Other results: Alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 45), international normalised ratio within normal limits, newborn screening and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the split bilirubin in two weeks and refer only if it remains elevated
options.rationale: A conjugated fraction this high is already abnormal and never physiological, so repeating it adds no information while consuming the operative window. Watchful repetition is appropriate for unconjugated jaundice in a thriving breastfed baby, which is a different problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Refer today to a paediatric liver unit for cholangiogram and possible Kasai
options.rationale: Pale stools with a conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total demand same day specialist referral, because the outcome of portoenterostomy falls sharply once the infant passes about 60 days of age and she is already 49 days old. Definitive assessment is an intraoperative cholangiogram, so referral is to a unit able to proceed to surgery on the same admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and arrange outpatient review in three weeks
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid is an adjunct for cholestatic symptoms once a cause is known and does nothing for an obstructed biliary tree. Starting it here creates the appearance of treatment while the operative window closes. (Source: GESA: Paediatric liver disease)

options.text: Arrange a sweat test and metabolic screen before making any surgical referral
options.rationale: Cystic fibrosis and metabolic disorders do belong in the wider cholestasis workup, but they are pursued in parallel with urgent referral rather than ahead of it. Sequencing them first delays the one diagnosis whose treatment is time critical. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Reassure that breast milk jaundice resolves and review again at three months
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and by definition has a normal conjugated fraction, so it cannot explain a conjugated bilirubin of 92 micromol/L or pale stools. Attributing conjugated jaundice to breastfeeding is the classic reason these infants present too late. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Any infant still jaundiced beyond 14 days of age needs a split bilirubin, and a conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total defines cholestasis that requires urgent investigation. Biliary atresia is the diagnosis that sets the clock, because the Kasai portoenterostomy restores bile drainage in most infants operated before about 60 days but in far fewer after 90 days, and those who fail drainage need transplantation in infancy. Pale stools and dark urine are the classic combination but are frequently missed because parents are not asked to look, and the baby otherwise thrives. The broader cholestasis workup for infection, metabolic and endocrine causes proceeds alongside referral rather than before it.
key_points: Jaundice beyond 14 days needs a split bilirubin, not reassurance
A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total is always pathological
Kasai outcomes deteriorate sharply beyond about 60 days of age
Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and cannot explain pale stools
Other cholestasis investigations run in parallel with urgent referral
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to photograph a nappy rather than describe the stool colour, because pale stools are reported as normal by most parents who have never been shown a comparison chart.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing confirmatory testing after strongly positive coeliac serology in a child still eating gluten
stem:
A 6 year old girl is reviewed in your general practice after her serology returned. She was tested because her weight has drifted from the 50th to the 10th centile over eighteen months and she complains of a sore tummy and feeling puffy after meals.

Her mother has autoimmune thyroid disease and has already bought gluten free products, asking whether she should start them today. The girl has continued her usual diet up to this appointment. Her abdomen is soft with no organomegaly and her iron studies show mild deficiency.

data_table.Growth: Weight tracking down from the 50th to the 10th centile over eighteen months, height on the 25th centile
data_table.Serology: Tissue transglutaminase IgA strongly positive at more than ten times the upper limit of normal, total IgA within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Keep gluten in her diet and refer for endoscopic small bowel biopsy
options.rationale: Histological confirmation remains the standard in Australian paediatric practice, and the mucosal changes begin to heal within weeks of gluten withdrawal, so removing gluten before biopsy can make the diagnosis impossible to secure. A lifelong dietary restriction warrants a firm diagnosis before it is imposed. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease clinical update)

options.text: Start a gluten free diet now and review her symptoms in six weeks
options.rationale: Symptomatic improvement on withdrawal is not diagnostic, because many children without coeliac disease feel better on the diet, and the change forecloses confirmatory biopsy. An empirical trial is reasonable only where coeliac disease has already been formally excluded. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease clinical update)

options.text: Repeat the antibody level after four weeks of a gluten free diet
options.rationale: Antibody titres fall with gluten withdrawal in both affected and unaffected children, so a falling level after four weeks discriminates nothing. Serial titres have a role in monitoring adherence once the diagnosis is established. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease clinical update)

options.text: Arrange HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing to confirm the diagnosis before referral
options.rationale: The genetic test is useful for its negative predictive value, since absence of both alleles effectively excludes the disease, but roughly half the general population carries one and a positive result confirms nothing. It cannot substitute for histology. (Source: RCH CPG: Coeliac disease)

options.text: Reassure the family and repeat her growth measurements in six months
options.rationale: Faltering growth with iron deficiency and a strongly positive antibody is an indication to complete the diagnostic pathway rather than to observe. Six months of further growth failure would be difficult to recover. (Source: RCH CPG: Coeliac disease)

explanation.summary: Coeliac disease in Australian children is diagnosed on the combination of positive serology and duodenal histology obtained while the child is still consuming gluten. The single most common preventable error is starting the diet before biopsy, because villous architecture recovers quickly and the family is then left choosing between an unconfirmed lifelong restriction and a gluten challenge that nobody wants to undertake. Tissue transglutaminase IgA is the screening test of choice but must be paired with a total IgA, since selective IgA deficiency is over ten times more common in coeliac disease and produces a falsely negative result. Associated autoimmune conditions, particularly type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease, raise the pre-test probability and appear frequently in the family history.
key_points: Biopsy is taken while the child is still eating gluten
Total IgA must accompany tissue transglutaminase IgA to exclude IgA deficiency
HLA typing excludes rather than confirms the diagnosis
Faltering growth and iron deficiency are common presenting features
Serology is used after diagnosis to monitor dietary adherence
explanation.pearls: If a family has already removed gluten before testing, a formal challenge of at least four weeks of gluten daily is needed before serology and biopsy become interpretable again.
